title: Ang 1399–1409: Bhatts on Ram Das, Arjan
hookLine: the poets' praise, where the name Waheguru rings out
tomorrow: Guru Nanak names the price of love's game. what is it?

cards: Right after you hit submit on something big, there's a silence where your stomach drops. Some grandmothers fill that silence with one word, said under the breath while they keep stirring the pot: Waheguru.
On ang 1402, a Bhatt named Gayand sings that same word over and over as a refrain, in praise of Guru Ram Das. That's the name from yesterday's question. Waheguru, Waheguru, Waheguru.

teach.b: Start with what Sikhs hear in the word. Wahe is a cry of wonder, the wow that comes before words, and guru is the one who brings light.
Together, Waheguru: the wondrous Lord, a name for God that Sikhs use in greeting, in prayer, and in a sigh.

teach.h: GAYAND SINGS IT TO RAM DAS.
teach.b: In Gayand's swayyas it comes again and again, and the praise of Guru Ram Das and the praise of the Wondrous One run into each other, because the Bhatts hear one light in the Guru.
Then the Bhatts move on to Guru Arjan and sing the same light again in the fifth Guru. So what does a word like that do on a nervous afternoon?
It isn't a bargain. Saying it doesn't fix how things turn out. It's wonder, said on purpose, at the exact moment fear wants the microphone.
People say it when something good happens and when nothing is certain yet, and both make sense: wonder doesn't wait for the results.
The Bhatts sang it to a Guru sitting right in front of them. A grandmother says it to a pot of dal. Same word, same turn: away from the knot in the stomach, toward the One.

how: Sikhs say Waheguru in prayer and in the greeting Waheguru ji ka Khalsa, Waheguru ji ki Fateh, and repeat it in naam simran, often with the breath; the Bhatts' swayyas are sung in kirtan.

o: where the Bhatts praise Ram Das and Waheguru rings
where Guru Nanak's love-game salok is found
where the dawn raga Prabhati begins

games.q: the Bhatts on Ram Das and Arjan — tap the pairs.

s: Waheguru is a word for luck
it's a name for God: wonder and praise, said in good times and uncertain ones.
in the Bhatts' swayyas, Waheguru comes as a refrain
Gayand sings it again and again in praise of Guru Ram Das.
Sikhs say Waheguru only in formal prayer
it comes in greeting, in prayer, and in a sigh at the stove.

games.q: your little brother is waiting on a test result and spiraling. he asks what to do with the waiting. what does Gayand's refrain point to?
o: turn the waiting into wonder: say the Name, then do the next small thing.
say Waheguru many times; that's how the result comes out right.
leave God out of it till the result comes, then give thanks after.
games.why: Waheguru isn't a bargain for a result. it's wonder said on purpose, before anything is known, and it turns toward the One.

practice: Close your eyes. On the breath in, think wahe; on the breath out, guru. Let the word ride the breath through the sit.
If you'd rather not use the word, just ride the breath; if you pray, this is one way Sikhs remember the Name.

wordCard.voice: Ang 1399. Where the Bhatts praise Guru Ram Das and Guru Arjan, and Gayand's refrain rings out: Waheguru.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: Waheguru, the wondrous Lord, sung as a refrain by the Bhatt Gayand on ang 1402.

carryVoice: Your line: waheguru. Wonder, said on purpose, before any of the results come in. Day done.
